Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Spatially displaced excitation contributes to the encoding of interrupted motion by the retinal direction-selective circuit" for further consideration by eLife. Your revised article has been reviewed by 3 reviewers, one of whom is a member of our Board of Reviewing Editors, and the evaluation has been overseen by Ronald Calabrese as the Senior Editor.

The reviewers appreciate the revisions to the modeling work, and all agreed that those strengthened the connection to function. Several issues remain that could be further clarified or expanded. (1) The impact of the non-DS region of the RF on encoding of motion direction (Figure 7D) is mentioned briefly in the text, but deserves a more complete treatment, especially as the effects seem substantial. (2) It is not clear why the lack of asymmetry of the dendrites along the preferred-null direction is emphasized and the bias in the direction of maximum excitatory input is relegated to the supplemental figure. The latter result appears to provide at least a partial mechanistic explanation for the bias in excitatory input, and it is not clear why it is not more prominent.

Reviewer #1:

This paper investigates the encoding of motion stimuli by On-Off directionally-selective ganglion cells. The paper introduces a new aspect of such motion sensitivity: the lack of directional selectivity in one part of the receptive field. Corresponding to this functional asymmetry, the glutamatergic excitatory input that the cells receive is not centered on the some, but instead is displaced towards the non-directional part of the receptive field. Modeling shows that this non-directional signal could help identify the position of a moving object, particularly as it emerges from occlusion. The work in the paper is new and interesting. The paper has improved considerable in revision – particularly the new modeling sections strengthen the conclusions about function quite a bit. I do not have any comments on the science itself. There are several places in which the writing could be clearer, as detailed below.

Paragraph starting on line 210. The text here I find confusing. First, you show that excitatory input shows an asymmetry that is in decent alignment with the preferred-null axis. Then you show that the dendrites do not exhibit an asymmetry along the preferred/null axis (at least as measured by branch points and dendritic length). But then Figure S2 and the text in this paragraph argues that there is a dendritic asymmetry in the direction of the largest EPSCs. I know these are not contradictory, but if you first distill each to a simple message then they appear to be. If I am representing these results correctly, some extra text to explain how they are consistent with each other would be helpful.

Lines 128-129: this is still a bit confusing – can you say something like "the preferred side is the side of the receptive field that a bar moving in the preferred direction enters first"

Lines 338-340: Another possibility here is that the kinetics of the bipolar signals do not differ substantially.

Lines 347-350: I would move "We reasoned.…" one sentence later; at present it comes in a sentence that summarizes previous findings.

Lines 406-407: Clarify that these drugs were used individually, not as a cocktail.

Lines 462-467: This paragraph seems out of place – can it go elsewhere?

Line 501: Can you add a sentence to define how the labeled-line decoder works? It would be helpful to have a little intuition here without having to go to the Methods.

Lines 513-515: some reference for what 3 degrees of visual angle means would help (e.g. give the RF sizes in degrees).

Figure 7: can you explain in the text a bit more about why you look at different baseline rates, and why the specific rates were chosen?

Figure 7: What is the "occlusion edge" trace in B? Also the text in this figure is very small and hard to read.

Lines 533-535: suggest emphasizing that simultaneous firing of two oppositely tuned DS cells is not expected for smooth motion. And simultaneous firing of two but not all four is not expected for non-motion contrast signals.

Reviewer #2:

In this research, Ding and colleagues present strong evidence that the excitatory input to OO DS RGCs from bipolar cells is strongly asymmetric, with strongest inputs occurring on the side opposite from the SAC inhibition. They performed careful studies to show that this was not due to spatial asymmetry in the DSGC morphology nor to ribbon synapse density. Using 'interrupted motion' stimuli, which are effectively local directional stimuli, they show that this asymmetry leads to a non-directional response on one side of the cell's RF. Last, they created a model to show that such firing patterns could be used to improve localization of edge position under the specific conditions of an edge emerging from behind an occlusion. They also show that such a set up could lead to an 'alarm response' indicating something interesting going on when local contrast changes, and may also improve the direction-selectivity of DS RGCs.

The strength of this work lies in its careful characterization of this property of ooDRGCs, and its tests of the mechanistic origins of this property. Some similar properties have been observed before, but not characterized with the detail here. The main challenge for this paper is to figure out what the functional significance of this finding is for the animal. This paper proposes a few grounded options, but they remain quite speculative.

I have a few comments, but I'd categorize them as perhaps important but not major. The authors addressed the critical points from the first review in their revised paper. I would have liked to see more about how this property affects direction-selectivity (the known property of these cells), since I suspect it's a large and important effect, but I'm satisfied with the panel presented.

The title refers to "the retinal ds circuit", but this paper only focuses on one of two DS RGC types, and primarily on only 1 (sometimes 2) of the four directions of that type. It seems as though these findings apply to "a retinal DS circuit", though this depends a bit on how one defines "the retinal DS circuit".

The authors have better grounded the modeling of reversed motion and 'alarm signals' in this revision. Since it is still difficult to connect mouse retina experiments to behavior, I wonder if the paper could benefit from a broader comparison in the discussion, since I believe the non-direction-selective responsiveness of motion detectors characterized here has also been found in other well-studied systems. In particular, I believe that DS V1 cells respond non-direction-selectively to local contrast changes, so that the logic of the modeling would apply there. Similarly, studies in flies have highlighted that their local motion detectors respond to local changes in contrast, and connected it to behavior in some cases (see Fisher et al., 2015; Haag et al., 2016; Gruntman et al., 2018; Wienecke et al., 2019; Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2018; Agrochao et al., 2020), so that the modeling logic should apply there, too. I think a discussion of how this modeling and proposed function might relate to similar features in other systems would strengthen the paper.

The authors chose to focus on a null result in Figure 2, in which dendritic arbors don't correlate strongly with direction-selectivity, but did not focus on the positive result shown in Supp 2, in which dendritic arbors correlated with the glutamatergic excitation field (S2D and E). I'm a little puzzled about why this positive result didn't warrant more discussion in the main text. Supp 2F shows no correlation between the dendritic and response RSIs, but crucially, this is only in the maximal direction for the response. If one computed the RSI for each of the 4 orientations in S2B, then the correlation would surely be significant (as it is in the other analyses in D and E). In that sense, this lack of correlation specifically in the max-opp orientation seems slightly second order. I agree that this plot can be interpreted to mean that it's not all due to dendritic arbor asymmetries, but it seems clear that the dendritic arbor has some influence on the location of the offset excitation in these neurons, so it's a little surprising that doesn't merit more attention.

L 598 typo "anther"

Note: I may have missed it, but I did not see any statement about the rawest data and analysis code being made available to readers, using Dryad and Github or another method. My impression was that this was mandatory.

Reviewer #3:

The revised manuscript is improved, and features more sophisticated modelling analysis. My first review emphasised a missing mechanistic explanation for the asymmetrical excitatory input received by this particular class of ON-OFF-DSGC. The authors have highlighted through analysis of dendritic morphology and a previously published EM volume that a simple structural basis for this asymmetry does not exists. They have not however investigated what the origin of the asymmetrical excitatory input is, which to this reviewers mind is a central ingredient of the work. The authors have however significantly improved their modelling work. My view of the manuscript remains unchanged, and I am left with a simple question – what is the basis of the asymmetyrical excitatory input received by this class of DSGC?

My major concern remains from the first round of review and has not been addressed in resubmission.

results.result: On-Off pDSGCs exhibit a spatially displaced glutamatergic receptive field toward the preferred side, as demonstrated by peripheral spot stimulation showing maximal spiking and EPSC responses on the preferred side that persist after blocking SAC inputs with DHβE and gabazine.
results.evaluation: Claims C13-C18 provide converging experimental evidence from both spiking recordings and voltage-clamp EPSC measurements showing spatial asymmetry in glutamatergic inputs. The persistence of this asymmetry after pharmacological blockade of SAC inputs (C16, C18) demonstrates that the displacement is not due to inhibitory circuit asymmetry. The data in Figures 1B-D with appropriate controls strongly support this core finding.

results.result: The displaced glutamatergic RF is partially but not fully explained by dendritic morphology. While dendritic arbors show no consistent bias along the preferred-null axis, there is a correlation between dendritic distribution and EPSC strength, though the RF center is displaced from the dendritic center for most cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C25 present morphological analysis showing that dendritic arbors are not systematically biased (C20-C21), yet there is partial correlation with EPSC patterns (C22-C23). The lack of positive correlation between EPSC bias and dendritic bias (C24) and the displacement of RF center from dendritic center (C25) indicate additional mechanisms beyond morphology. The data in Figure 2 support these conclusions with appropriate quantification.

results.result: The spatial asymmetry in glutamatergic inputs arises from non-uniform EPSC density across the dendritic field rather than from differential bipolar cell ribbon synapse density, as demonstrated by higher EPSC density on the displaced side while ribbon density shows no gradient.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C27 show differential EPSC density normalized by dendritic length (Figure 3E), while C28 demonstrates no gradient in bipolar ribbon density from EM reconstruction (Figure 4D-F). This combination of functional and anatomical data effectively rules out presynaptic density as the mechanism and points to postsynaptic or synaptic strength differences. The experimental approaches are complementary and well-controlled.

results.result: Glutamatergic EPSC kinetics (latency, rise time, decay time) do not differ substantially across the preferred-null motion axis, suggesting that bipolar cell signal kinetics are uniform across the pDSGC dendritic field.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C31 present kinetic analysis showing no significant differences in EPSC temporal properties across the RF (Figure 4G-I). This negative result is important as it rules out kinetic gradients as a mechanism for direction selectivity in On-Off pDSGCs, contrasting with On DSGCs. The analysis is thorough with multiple kinetic parameters examined under different pharmacological conditions.

results.result: Occluded motion stimuli evoke both preferred and null-direction spiking responses when the bar travels on the preferred side of the RF, and this regional asymmetry persists after blocking SAC inputs and other inhibitory mechanisms, demonstrating that the displaced glutamatergic RF drives these responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C33-C36 and C38-C39 present comprehensive pharmacological dissection showing that null-direction responses during occluded motion persist after blocking cholinergic, GABAergic (GABAA and GABAC), glycinergic, and gap junction signaling (Figures 5B-C, Figure 5—supplement 1H-K). This extensive pharmacology effectively isolates the glutamatergic contribution and supports the conclusion that the displaced excitatory RF underlies these responses.

results.result: Anterior-preferring DSGCs (aDSGCs) also exhibit null-direction responses to occluded motion similar to pDSGCs, indicating that RF displacement toward the preferred side is a general feature of On-Off DSGCs.
results.evaluation: Claim C40 extends the main finding to another DSGC subtype using calcium imaging (Figure 5H, Figure 5—supplement 2D). This generalization strengthens the overall conclusion, though the evidence is based on calcium signals rather than direct electrophysiology. The similarity in response patterns between pDSGCs and aDSGCs supports the inference of RF displacement in aDSGCs.

results.result: The null-direction response during interrupted motion depends on the spatial position from which the moving edge emerges within the RF, not on the previous motion trajectory, as demonstrated by emergent bar experiments showing position-dependent spiking.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C42 present emergent bar experiments (Figure 6) that dissociate the effects of motion history from spatial position. The systematic increase in null-direction spiking as the bar emerges from more preferred-side locations provides clear evidence that spatial position within the RF, not motion history, determines the response. This is a well-designed control experiment.

results.result: Computational modeling demonstrates that synchronous firing between oppositely tuned DSGCs during interrupted motion substantially improves spatial position estimation (>80% error reduction at low speeds, ~40% at high speeds) while transiently degrading direction estimation, suggesting a trade-off that prioritizes position encoding at motion interruption sites.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C50 present a comprehensive computational model with biologically realistic parameters derived from experimental data (Figure 7, Figure 7—supplement 1). The model makes specific quantitative predictions about position and direction decoding accuracy. The modeling approach is sound with appropriate parameter estimation, though the functional interpretation remains speculative. The quantitative results (C47-C49) are clearly stated and supported by the simulations.

results.result: The displaced RF does not improve detection of non-directional contrast changes compared to symmetric RFs; directed motion is required for improved position estimation because null-direction signals only occur in a small region on the preferred side, yielding a spatially constrained population signal.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C54 address an important control question about whether RF displacement benefits static contrast detection. The negative result (C51-C52) and the mechanistic explanation (C53-C54) are logical and supported by the modeling framework. This helps clarify the specific conditions under which the displaced RF provides functional benefits.

results.result: A coincidence detection model shows that synchronous firing between oppositely tuned DSGC subtypes during interrupted motion can be detected with >99% accuracy at low background firing rates, potentially serving as an alarm signal for motion discontinuities.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C56 present a coincidence detection analysis (Figure 7H) showing high detection accuracy under biologically realistic noise conditions. The ROC analysis is appropriate for assessing detector performance. However, C57's interpretation as an 'alarm signal' is speculative and not directly tested. The detection accuracy results are solid, but the functional interpretation requires caution.

results.result: Cells with more spatially separated excitatory and inhibitory receptive fields show greater direction selectivity during full-field motion.
results.evaluation: Claim C32 presents a correlation analysis (Figure 7—supplement 1L) showing that spatial separation of excitatory and inhibitory RFs correlates with direction selectivity. This supports the idea that the displaced excitatory RF may enhance direction selectivity during full-field motion by optimizing the timing of excitation and inhibition. The correlation is clearly demonstrated.

results.result: The study reveals that On-Off DSGCs exploit different mechanisms under different stimulus conditions: full-field motion maximizes SAC-mediated inhibition for direction selectivity, while occluded motion reduces SAC contribution allowing the displaced excitatory RF to dominate, with responses determined by both the extent and location of RF activation.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C60 synthesize the main findings into a coherent framework showing stimulus-dependent circuit mechanisms. This is well-supported by the experimental data showing different response patterns to full-field versus occluded motion (Figures 5-6) and the pharmacological dissection demonstrating reduced SAC contribution during partial RF activation. The conceptual framework is logical and data-driven.

results.result: The gradient in glutamatergic current density may arise from varying synaptic strengths, heterogeneous membrane properties, or contributions from Vglut3+ amacrine cells.
results.evaluation: Claim C61 presents plausible mechanistic hypotheses supported by citations, but these mechanisms are not directly tested in the current study. The claim appropriately acknowledges uncertainty ('may arise from'), but without experimental evidence distinguishing among these possibilities, the specific mechanisms remain speculative. Further experiments would be needed to evaluate these hypotheses.

results.result: During interrupted motion, null-direction responses transiently improve location encoding at the expense of direction encoding, potentially reflecting greater behavioral need for positional information of emerging objects and providing an alarm signal for discontinuous motion.
results.evaluation: Claim C62 is supported by the modeling results (Figure 7), but C63-C64 are speculative interpretations about behavioral relevance and functional significance. While the computational results clearly show the position-direction trade-off, the claims about 'greater need' and 'alarm signal' function are not directly tested and represent hypotheses about ethological relevance. These functional interpretations require behavioral validation.

results.result: The encoding of emerging object location by On-Off DSGCs may benefit collicular sensorimotor decisions, and while other RGC types (W3, HD-RGCs) may encode position, this information may not be available to circuits receiving On-Off DSGC inputs due to divergent projection patterns.
results.evaluation: Claims C73, C77-C78 present speculation about functional roles and circuit-level implications based on known projection patterns (citations provided). While the reasoning is logical and grounded in anatomical knowledge, these claims about downstream function and circuit-specific information availability are not directly tested. The speculation is reasonable but requires experimental validation of downstream processing and behavioral relevance.

results.result: Background claims establishing well-known properties of DSGCs and the direction-selective circuit, including the role of SAC inhibition, asymmetric wiring, and On-Off DSGC morphology.
results.evaluation: Claims C5-C12 present established knowledge about the direction-selective circuit supported by appropriate citations to classic and recent literature. These provide necessary context for the current work. C12 is additionally supported by Figure 1A showing the circuit diagram. These background claims are well-established in the field.

results.result: The findings parallel observations in other systems where population activity resolves single-cell ambiguities, specific stimulus patterns trigger context-specific encoding, and local motion detection can be performed by neurons with wide receptive fields, as seen in fly visual systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C69 contextualize the findings within broader principles of visual processing and draw parallels to work in other species, particularly flies. These comparisons are supported by appropriate citations and help place the work in a broader conceptual framework. The parallels drawn are reasonable and well-supported by the cited literature.

results.result: Discussion of On-Off DSGC projection patterns, comparison with other RGC types for spatial encoding, and speculation about functional roles and complementary information encoding, with acknowledgment that understanding requires further investigation of downstream processing and behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 present established anatomical knowledge (supported by citations), while C74-C76 and C79-C82 involve speculation about functional roles and comparisons with other cell types. The speculation is grounded in known anatomy and prior modeling work (citations provided), but the functional claims about complementary encoding and downstream benefits are not directly tested.
